encoded_text: Having both a Safe Harbor agreement and an Incidental Take Permit (ITP) is entirely permissible—they are not mutually exclusive. Related but separate, an ITP addresses incidental takes that may occur during otherwise lawful activities on the property. The explicit language of the policy makes clear that a landowner "can have either a Safe Harbor agreement or an Incidental Take Permit, or both." This framework, developed by the Clinton Administration in 1999, relies on the "enhancement of survival" provision found in Section 1539(a)(1)(A) and was designed to give landowners flexible tools to engage in conservation while retaining productive use of their land.
context: The "Safe Harbor" agreement is a voluntary agreement between the private landowner and FWS. The policy relies on the "enhancement of survival" provision of Section §1539(a)(1)(A). A landowner can have either a "Safe Harbor" agreement or an Incidental Take Permit, or both. question: Are Safe Harbor agreements and ITPs mutually exclusive?

encoded_text: Filament size and voltage level share an inverse relationship. Lower voltage lamps require a thicker filament to deliver the same power rating. This is because at lower voltages, a greater current must flow to achieve the exact same wattage, necessitating a larger cross-sectional area in the filament. The thicker filament can also operate at higher temperatures for the same rated lifetime before it evaporates, which explains why lower voltage lamps — such as 30-volt train lighting lamps — produce noticeably more lumens per watt. Conversely, higher voltage lamps use thinner filaments that run cooler and yield comparatively fewer lumens per watt, as seen when comparing a 230-volt lamp's roughly 12.8 lumens per watt against a 120-volt lamp's approximately 17.1 lumens per watt.
context: Lamps designed for different voltages have different luminous efficacy. For example, a 100-watt, 120-volt lamp will produce about 17.1 lumens per watt. A lamp with the same rated lifetime but designed for 230 V would produce only around 12.8 lumens per watt, and a similar lamp designed for 30 volts (train lighting) would produce as much as 19.8 lumens per watt. Lower voltage lamps have a thicker filament, for the same power rating. They can run hotter for the same lifetime before the filament evaporates.
question: How does filament size relate to voltage level?

question: What type of energy due photoelectrons emitted due to the photoelectric effect have?

encoded_text: Heat can be fully converted into work in a reversible isothermal expansion of an ideal gas. According to the first law of thermodynamics, energy cannot be created or destroyed, so during this specific process, all absorbed heat energy is transformed entirely into mechanical work. However, this complete conversion only applies to this particular type of process. For cyclic processes of practical interest, such as those in heat engines, the second law of thermodynamics dictates that some energy is inevitably lost as waste heat, limiting the available energy that can actually perform work.
context: For "closed systems" with no external source or sink of energy, the first law of thermodynamics states that a system's energy is constant unless energy is transferred in or out by mechanical work or heat, and that no energy is lost in transfer. This means that it is impossible to create or destroy energy. While heat can always be fully converted into work in a reversible isothermal expansion of an ideal gas, for cyclic processes of practical interest in heat engines the second law of thermodynamics states that the system doing work always loses some energy as waste heat. This creates a limit to the amount of heat energy that can do work in a cyclic process, a limit called the available energy. Mechanical and other forms of energy can be transformed in the other direction into thermal energy without such limitations. The total energy of a system can be calculated by adding up all forms of energy in the system.
question: What can be fully converted into work in a reversible isothermal expansion of an ideal gas?

encoded_text: You can think of homeostasis as being very similar to a common household thermostat. The underlying principle in both cases is negative feedback: when a value drifts from its set-point, the system detects the error and activates a corrective response to bring things back to normal. Maintaining homeostasis is a crucial function of the brain. The basic principle that underlies homeostasis is negative feedback: any time a parameter diverges from its set-point, sensors generate an error signal that evokes a response that causes the parameter to shift back toward its optimum value. (This principle is widely used in engineering, for example in the control of temperature using a thermostat.)

Like all carbohydrates, when it is metabolized it can produce four Calories (kilocalories) of energy per gram. However, in most circumstances it accounts for less than that because of its limited absorption and digestibility. Dietary fiber consists mainly of cellulose, a large carbohydrate polymer which is indigestible as humans do not have the required enzymes to disassemble it. There are two subcategories: soluble and insoluble fiber. Whole grains, fruits (especially plums, prunes, and figs), and vegetables are good sources of dietary fiber. There are many health benefits of a high-fiber diet. Dietary fiber helps reduce the chance of gastrointestinal problems such as constipation and diarrhea by increasing the weight and size of stool and softening it. Insoluble fiber, found in whole wheat flour, nuts and vegetables, especially stimulates peristalsis – the rhythmic muscular contractions of the intestines, which move digesta along the digestive tract. Soluble fiber, found in oats, peas, beans, and many fruits, dissolves in water in the intestinal tract to produce a gel that slows the movement of food through the intestines. This may help lower blood glucose levels because it can slow the absorption of sugar. Additionally, fiber, perhaps especially that from whole grains, is thought to possibly help lessen insulin spikes, and therefore reduce the risk of type 2 diabetes. The link between increased fiber consumption and a decreased risk of colorectal cancer is still uncertain.

encoded_text: Most notably, two experimentally verified effects of vacuum fluctuations are **spontaneous emission** and the **Lamb shift**. Vacuum fluctuations are an essential and ubiquitous part of quantum field theory. Some experimentally verified effects of vacuum fluctuations include spontaneous emission and the Lamb shift. Coulomb's law and the electric potential in vacuum near an electric charge are modified.
question: What is a verified effect of vacuum fluctuation?

encoded_text: Understanding the shortcomings of existing measurement tools was the primary motivation behind the creation of the SASO (Sell Assessment of Sexual Orientation). Rather than positioning itself as a definitive answer, the SASO was intentionally meant to provoke further discussion and debate about the best ways to measure sexual orientation. All of these design choices reflect a commitment to more nuanced, comprehensive approaches to understanding human sexuality.

encoded_text: From early accounts, ether was originally thought to be composed of a rigid, indestructible material that seamlessly filled the heavens. Over time, the concept evolved — borrowing from the Stoic idea of pneuma, aether came to be understood as a rarefied form of air, which is actually the origin of its name. It served as a theoretical medium believed to permeate both terrestrial and celestial realms, through which light was thought to propagate. Later, it also informed Isaac Newton's work on refraction and radiant heat.
context: While outer space provides the most rarefied example of a naturally occurring partial vacuum, the heavens were originally thought to be seamlessly filled by a rigid indestructible material called aether. Borrowing somewhat from the pneuma of Stoic physics, aether came to be regarded as the rarefied air from which it took its name, (see Aether (mythology)). Early theories of light posited a ubiquitous terrestrial and celestial medium through which light propagated. Additionally, the concept informed Isaac Newton's explanations of both refraction and of radiant heat. 19th century experiments into this luminiferous aether attempted to detect a minute drag on the Earth's orbit. While the Earth does, in fact, move through a relatively dense medium in comparison to that of interstellar space, the drag is so minuscule that it could not be detected. In 1912, astronomer Henry Pickering commented: "While the interstellar absorbing medium may be simply the ether, [it] is characteristic of a gas, and free gaseous molecules are certainly there".
question: What was ether originally thought to be made of?

encoded_text: Rising evidence from molecular studies shows that chloroplasts in early vegetation appeared through a process known as endosymbiosis. In this process, ancient eukaryotic cells that had already acquired mitochondria engulfed cyanobacterial-like organisms. Slowly, rather than being digested, these cyanobacteria became fully integrated into their host cells over evolutionary time, eventually transforming into chloroplasts — the organelles responsible for photosynthesis in algae and plants. Even more fascinating, some algae later underwent additional rounds of endosymbiosis, where a eukaryote engulfed another eukaryotic alga, giving rise to "second-generation" plastids through what is called secondary endosymbiosis.
context: The ancestors of modern bacteria were unicellular microorganisms that were the first forms of life to appear on Earth, about 4 billion years ago. For about 3 billion years, most organisms were microscopic, and bacteria and archaea were the dominant forms of life. In 2008, fossils of macroorganisms were discovered and named as the Francevillian biota. Although bacterial fossils exist, such as stromatolites, their lack of distinctive morphology prevents them from being used to examine the history of bacterial evolution, or to date the time of origin of a particular bacterial species. However, gene sequences can be used to reconstruct the bacterial phylogeny, and these studies indicate that bacteria diverged first from the archaeal/eukaryotic lineage. Bacteria were also involved in the second great evolutionary divergence, that of the archaea and eukaryotes. Here, eukaryotes resulted from the entering of ancient bacteria into endosymbiotic associations with the ancestors of eukaryotic cells, which were themselves possibly related to the Archaea. This involved the engulfment by proto-eukaryotic cells of alphaproteobacterial symbionts to form either mitochondria or hydrogenosomes, which are still found in all known Eukarya (sometimes in highly reduced form, e.g. in ancient "amitochondrial" protozoa). Later on, some eukaryotes that already contained mitochondria also engulfed cyanobacterial-like organisms. This led to the formation of chloroplasts in algae and plants. There are also some algae that originated from even later endosymbiotic events. Here, eukaryotes engulfed a eukaryotic algae that developed into a "second-generation" plastid. This is known as secondary endosymbiosis.
question: How did chloroplast appear in first vegetation?

encoded_text: With its roots deeply embedded in ancient Greek philosophy, Christian idealism was often grounded in **Neoplatonism**. Christian theologians readily adopted Neoplatonic concepts to support their idealist views, though the rise of Aristotelian scholasticism from the 12th century onward introduced competing philosophical influences. Several modern religious movements, for example the organizations within the New Thought Movement and the Unity Church, may be said to have a particularly idealist orientation. The theology of Christian Science includes a form of idealism: it teaches that all that truly exists is God and God's ideas; that the world as it appears to the senses is a distortion of the underlying spiritual reality, a distortion that may be corrected (both conceptually and in terms of human experience) through a reorientation (spiritualization) of thought.
question: In what philosophy was Christian idealism often rooted?

encoded_text: Chronic pain is sometimes referred to as "persistent" pain. The two terms are frequently used interchangeably in medical contexts to describe pain that lasts beyond the expected period of healing. Generally, this means pain persisting for more than three to six months, although exact definitions can vary among practitioners and researchers.
context: Pain is usually transitory, lasting only until the noxious stimulus is removed or the underlying damage or pathology has healed, but some painful conditions, such as rheumatoid arthritis, peripheral neuropathy, cancer and idiopathic pain, may persist for years. Pain that lasts a long time is called chronic or persistent, and pain that resolves quickly is called acute. Traditionally, the distinction between acute and chronic pain has relied upon an arbitrary interval of time from onset; the two most commonly used markers being 3 months and 6 months since the onset of pain, though some theorists and researchers have placed the transition from acute to chronic pain at 12 months.:93 Others apply acute to pain that lasts less than 30 days, chronic to pain of more than six months' duration, and subacute to pain that lasts from one to six months. A popular alternative definition of chronic pain, involving no arbitrarily fixed durations, is "pain that extends beyond the expected period of healing". Chronic pain may be classified as cancer pain or else as benign.
question: What might chronic pain sometimes be referred to as?

encoded_text: Linguistic nationalism is the primary reason the term "Serbo-Croatian" is controversial today. The core issue is the deeply held belief that a distinct nation should have its own distinctly named language. After the breakup of Yugoslavia, the newly independent states — Croatia, Serbia, Bosnia and Herzegovina, and Montenegro — each sought to establish their own officially named language variety as a marker of sovereign identity. Even though these varieties remain mutually intelligible and share a common linguistic foundation, the political desire to align language with national identity has made the umbrella term "Serbo-Croatian" unwelcome to many. For practical purposes, alternative labels such as "Bosnian/Croatian/Serbian" (BCS) have been adopted in certain political and legal contexts, including at the Hague War Crimes tribunal, though no single succinct replacement has gained universal acceptance.
context: Throughout the history of the South Slavs, the vernacular, literary, and written languages (e.g. Chakavian, Kajkavian, Shtokavian) of the various regions and ethnicities developed and diverged independently. Prior to the 19th century, they were collectively called "Illyric", "Slavic", "Slavonian", "Bosnian", "Dalmatian", "Serbian" or "Croatian". As such, the term Serbo-Croatian was first used by Jacob Grimm in 1824, popularized by the Vienna philologist Jernej Kopitar in the following decades, and accepted by Croatian Zagreb grammarians in 1854 and 1859. At that time, Serb and Croat lands were still part of the Ottoman and Austrian Empires. Officially, the language was called variously Serbo-Croat, Croato-Serbian, Serbian and Croatian, Croatian and Serbian, Serbian or Croatian, Croatian or Serbian. Unofficially, Serbs and Croats typically called the language "Serbian" or "Croatian", respectively, without implying a distinction between the two, and again in independent Bosnia and Herzegovina, "Bosnian", "Croatian", and "Serbian" were considered to be three names of a single official language. Croatian linguist Dalibor Brozović advocated the term Serbo-Croatian as late as 1988, claiming that in an analogy with Indo-European, Serbo-Croatian does not only name the two components of the same language, but simply charts the limits of the region in which it is spoken and includes everything between the limits (‘Bosnian’ and ‘Montenegrin’). Today, use of the term "Serbo-Croatian" is controversial due to the prejudice that nation and language must match. It is still used for lack of a succinct alternative, though alternative names have been used, such as Bosnian/Croatian/Serbian (BCS), which is often seen in political contexts such as the Hague War Crimes tribunal.
question: For what reason is the term "Serbo-Croatian" controversial today?

encoded_text: Lossless audio compression produces a representation of digital data that decompresses to an exact digital duplicate of the original audio stream. Put another way, it preserves perfect fidelity to the source material, unlike lossy compression techniques such as Vorbis and MP3, which discard some data to achieve smaller file sizes. Typical compression ratios for lossless formats land around 50–60% of the original size, with codecs like FLAC, Shorten, and TTA using linear prediction to estimate the signal's spectrum and improve compression efficiency.
context: Lossless audio compression produces a representation of digital data that decompress to an exact digital duplicate of the original audio stream, unlike playback from lossy compression techniques such as Vorbis and MP3. Lossless compression is unable to attain high compression ratios due to the complexity of waveforms and the rapid changes in sound forms. Codecs like FLAC, Shorten and TTA use linear prediction to estimate the spectrum of the signal. Many of these algorithms use convolution with the filter [-1 1] to slightly whiten or flatten the spectrum, thereby allowing traditional lossless compression to work more efficiently. The process is reversed upon decompression.

encoded_text: Just as its Greek origins suggest—meaning "standing still"—homeostasis is defined as the ability of an animal to regulate the internal environment of its body, keeping various bodily parameters within a limited range of variation. These parameters include temperature, water content, salt concentration in the bloodstream, blood glucose levels, and blood oxygen levels. The pioneering physiologist Claude Bernard referred to this regulated internal environment as the *milieu intérieur*. The fundamental principle underlying homeostasis is negative feedback: whenever a parameter diverges from its set-point, sensors generate an error signal that evokes a corrective response, pushing the parameter back toward its optimum value. A familiar engineering analogy for this process is the thermostat, which uses the same negative feedback principle to maintain a desired temperature.

encoded_text: A CCA (Candidate Conservation Agreement With Assurances) helps protect private landowners by providing them with regulatory certainty regarding species that are currently unlisted but may become threatened or endangered in the future. These assurances guarantee that if the species later becomes officially listed under the Endangered Species Act, the landowner will not be required to take on any additional conservation obligations beyond what was originally agreed upon in the CCA. In essence, the agreement acts as a safeguard, ensuring that a landowner's voluntary conservation efforts will not lead to greater regulatory burdens down the road. This creates a powerful incentive for private landowners to proactively engage in habitat conservation without fear of future penalties or increased restrictions.
context: The Candidate Conservation Agreement is closely related to the "Safe Harbor" agreement, the main difference is that the Candidate Conservation Agreements With Assurances(CCA) are meant to protect unlisted species by providing incentives to private landowners and land managing agencies to restore, enhance or maintain habitat of unlisted species which are declining and have the potential to become threatened or endangered if critical habitat is not protected. encoded_text: Using Planck constant values derived from the Josephson effect and quantum Hall effect to test those same theories would result in a **circular argument**. Because these methods depend on the theoretical foundations of the Josephson effect and the quantum Hall effect, the values they produce inherently assume the theories are correct. Trying to then use those values as evidence supporting the theories means you are essentially presupposing the conclusion you are attempting to prove. The reasoning loops back on itself — the derived constant assumes theoretical accuracy, and the theoretical accuracy is then "confirmed" by the derived constant. Fortunately, researchers can rely on other independent statistical methods to test these theories without falling into this logical trap.
context: The theoretical difficulties arise from the fact that all of the methods except the X-ray crystal density method rely on the theoretical basis of the Josephson effect and the quantum Hall effect. If these theories are slightly inaccurate – though there is no evidence at present to suggest they are – the methods would not give accurate values for the Planck constant. More importantly, the values of the Planck constant obtained in this way cannot be used as tests of the theories without falling into a circular argument. Fortunately, there are other statistical ways of testing the theories, and the theories have yet to be refuted.
question: Using Planck constant values from these effects would lead to what logical issue?

encoded_text: Starting from an offseason roster limit of 90 players, each NFL team must cut down to **53 players** for the regular season. Preseason exhibition games, typically held in August, serve as the evaluation period during which coaches assess their roster and make the necessary cuts to reach that 53-player limit.
context: Compared to other team sports, the National Football League preseason is very structured. Every NFL team plays exactly four pre-season exhibition games a year, two at home and two away, with the exception of two teams each year who play a fifth game, the Pro Football Hall of Fame Game. These exhibition games, most of which are held in the month of August, are played for the purpose of helping coaches narrow down the roster from the offseason limit of 90 players to the regular-season limit of 53 players. While the scheduling formula is not as rigid for preseason games as they are for the regular season, there are numerous restrictions and traditions that limit the choices of preseason opponents; teams are also restricted on what days and times they can play these games. Split-squad games, a practice common in baseball and hockey, where a team that is scheduled to play two games on the same day splits their team into two squads, are prohibited. The NFL has played exhibition games in Europe, Japan, Canada, Australia (including the American Bowl in 1999) and Mexico to spread the league's popularity (a game of this type was proposed for China but, due to financial and logistical problems, was eventually canceled). The league has tacitly forbidden the playing of non-league opponents, with the last interleague game having come in 1972 and the last game against a team other than an NFL team (the all-NFL rookie College All-Stars) was held in 1976. Exhibition games are quite unpopular with many fans, who resent having to pay regular-season prices for two home exhibition games as part of a season-ticket package. Numerous lawsuits have been brought by fans and classes of fans against the NFL or its member teams regarding this practice, but none have been successful in halting it.[citation needed] The Pro Bowl, traditionally played after the end of the NFL season (since 2011 is played the week prior to the Super Bowl), is also considered an exhibition game.

encoded_text: Natural changes in elevation cause the temperature to decrease. Specifically, a rise from sea level into the upper regions of the atmosphere results in cooling, a phenomenon explained by the adiabatic lapse rate. As air ascends—particularly when mountain chains like the Alps force prevailing winds upward—it expands in volume, and this expansion comes at the cost of a proportionate loss of temperature. This cooling process is often accompanied by precipitation in the form of snow or rain, which is why the Alps effectively divide Europe's weather into a wet north and a dry south.
context: The Alps are a classic example of what happens when a temperate area at lower altitude gives way to higher-elevation terrain. Elevations around the world that have cold climates similar to those of the polar regions have been called Alpine. A rise from sea level into the upper regions of the atmosphere causes the temperature to decrease (see adiabatic lapse rate). The effect of mountain chains on prevailing winds is to carry warm air belonging to the lower region into an upper zone, where it expands in volume at the cost of a proportionate loss of temperature, often accompanied by precipitation in the form of snow or rain. The height of the Alps is sufficient to divide the weather patterns in Europe into a wet north and a dry south because moisture is sucked from the air as it flows over the high peaks.
question: What causes the temperature to decrease?

encoded_text: Starting from Lagrange's theorem, finite groups of order p—where p is a prime number—are necessarily cyclic (abelian) groups Zp. encoded_text: Antiochus of Ascalon was the philosopher who grew disillusioned with Academic Skepticism, rejecting it around 90 BCE in favor of Neoplatonism. He marked a significant turning point in the history of the Academy, which had embraced skepticism under Arcesilaus.
context: The Epicureans and the Cynics rejected public offices and civic service, which amounted to a rejection of the polis itself, the defining institution of the Greek world. Epicurus promoted atomism and an asceticism based on freedom from pain as its ultimate goal. Cynics such as Diogenes of Sinope rejected all material possessions and social conventions (nomos) as unnatural and useless. The Cyrenaics meanwhile, embraced hedonism, arguing that pleasure was the only true good. Stoicism, founded by Zeno of Citium, taught that virtue was sufficient for eudaimonia as it would allow one to live in accordance with Nature or Logos. Zeno became extremely popular, the Athenians set up a gold statue of him and Antigonus II Gonatas invited him to the Macedonian court. The philosophical schools of Aristotle (the Peripatetics of the Lyceum) and Plato (Platonism at the Academy) also remained influential. The academy would eventually turn to Academic Skepticism under Arcesilaus until it was rejected by Antiochus of Ascalon (c. 90 BCE) in favor of Neoplatonism. Hellenistic philosophy, had a significant influence on the Greek ruling elite. Examples include Athenian statesman Demetrius of Phaleron, who had studied in the lyceum; the Spartan king Cleomenes III who was a student of the Stoic Sphairos of Borysthenes and Antigonus II who was also a well known Stoic. question: Who rejected Academic Skepticism in favor of Neoplatonism?

encoded_text: Crucially, the light emitted by an incandescent bulb does not appear white because its spectrum doesn't align well with the sensitivity of the human eye. Essentially, tungsten filaments operate at temperatures far below the ideal ~6,300 °C needed for the most efficient visible light production, so most of the energy they radiate falls in the infrared range rather than the visible spectrum. Even the small portion of radiation that is visible skews heavily toward warmer, reddish tones due to the relatively low operating temperature of the filament compared to what would be needed for balanced, white light — meaning incandescent bulbs are highly inefficient at producing useful visible light, with a theoretical upper luminous efficacy of only about 52 lumens per watt at tungsten's melting point.
context: The spectrum emitted by a blackbody radiator at temperatures of incandescent bulbs does not match the sensitivity characteristics of the human eye; the light emitted does not appear white, and most is not in the range of wavelengths at which the eye is most sensitive. Tungsten filaments radiate mostly infrared radiation at temperatures where they remain solid – below 3,695 K (3,422 °C; 6,191 °F). Donald L. Klipstein explains it this way: "An ideal thermal radiator produces visible light most efficiently at temperatures around 6,300 °C (6,600 K; 11,400 °F). Even at this high temperature, a lot of the radiation is either infrared or ultraviolet, and the theoretical luminous efficacy (LER) is 95 lumens per watt." No known material can be used as a filament at this ideal temperature, which is hotter than the sun's surface. An upper limit for incandescent lamp luminous efficacy (LER) is around 52 lumens per watt, the theoretical value emitted by tungsten at its melting point.
question: What is the flaw in the color of light produced by an incandescent bulb?

encoded_text: Looking at this topic, Whitehead stated that it is not philosophically or ontologically sound to think that a person is the same from one second to the next. He acknowledged that everyday language encourages us to treat people and objects as fundamentally unchanging substances, since it would be impractical to give each moment of a person's life a different proper name. However, he argued that this convenience of speech should not be confused with reality. Whitehead emphasized that what we call "material substances" or "essences" are really just generalized descriptions of a continuum of particular, concrete processes. He used the relatable example that no one questions a ten-year-old is quite different by the time they reach thirty, and in many ways is not the same person at all. Extending this logic, Whitehead maintained that the same principle applies on a moment-to-moment basis — each thing is fundamentally a different thing from what it was an instant ago. The belief in moment-to-moment sameness, in his view, stems from the limitations of language and habitual materialistic thinking rather than from any genuine philosophical foundation.
context: Whitehead pointed to the limitations of language as one of the main culprits in maintaining a materialistic way of thinking, and acknowledged that it may be difficult to ever wholly move past such ideas in everyday speech. After all, each moment of each person's life can hardly be given a different proper name, and it is easy and convenient to think of people and objects as remaining fundamentally the same things, rather than constantly keeping in mind that each thing is a different thing from what it was a moment ago. Yet the limitations of everyday living and everyday speech should not prevent people from realizing that "material substances" or "essences" are a convenient generalized description of a continuum of particular, concrete processes. No one questions that a ten-year-old person is quite different by the time he or she turns thirty years old, and in many ways is not the same person at all; Whitehead points out that it is not philosophically or ontologically sound to think that a person is the same from one second to the next.

encoded_text: On two occasions — first in 1592 and again in 1597 — Toyotomi Hideyoshi mobilized an army of 160,000 troops to send to Korea. This massive force was composed of both peasants and samurai, deployed as part of Hideyoshi's ambitious plan to invade China by way of the Korean peninsula.
context: In 1592, and again in 1597, Toyotomi Hideyoshi, aiming to invade China (唐入り) through Korea, mobilized an army of 160,000 peasants and samurai and deployed them to Korea. (See Hideyoshi's invasions of Korea, Chōsen-seibatsu (朝鮮征伐?). Taking advantage of arquebus mastery and extensive wartime experience from the Sengoku period, Japanese samurai armies made major gains in most of Korea. Kato Kiyomasa advanced to Orangkai territory (present-day Manchuria) bordering Korea to the northeast and crossed the border into Manchuria, but withdrew after retaliatory attacks from the Jurchens there, as it was clear he had outpaced the rest of the Japanese invasion force. A few of the more famous samurai generals of this war were Katō Kiyomasa, Konishi Yukinaga, and Shimazu Yoshihiro. Shimazu Yoshihiro led some 7,000 samurai and, despite being heavily outnumbered, defeated a host of allied Ming and Korean forces at the Battle of Sacheon in 1598, near the conclusion of the campaigns. Yoshihiro was feared as Oni-Shimazu ("Shimazu ogre") and his nickname spread across not only Korea but to Ming Dynasty China. In spite of the superiority of Japanese land forces, ultimately the two expeditions failed (though they did devastate the Korean landmass) from factors such as Korean naval superiority (which, led by Admiral Yi Sun-shin, harassed Japanese supply lines continuously throughout the wars, resulting in supply shortages on land), the commitment of sizeable Ming forces to Korea, Korean guerrilla actions, the underestimation of resistance by Japanese commanders (in the first campaign of 1592, Korean defenses on land were caught unprepared, under-trained, and under-armed; they were rapidly overrun, with only a limited number of successfully resistant engagements against the more-experienced and battle-hardened Japanese forces - in the second campaign of 1597, Korean and Ming forces proved to be a far more difficult challenge and, with the support of continued Korean naval superiority, limited Japanese gains to parts southeastern Korea), and wavering Japanese commitment to the campaigns as the wars dragged on. The final death blow to the Japanese campaigns in Korea came with Hideyoshi's death in late 1598 and the recall of all Japanese forces in Korea by the Council of Five Elders (established by Hideyoshi to oversee the transition from his regency to that of his son Hideyori).
question: How many troops did Toyotomi Hideyoshi send to Korea?

encoded_text: The Latin word for dog is **Canis**. As recorded by the taxonomist Linnaeus in his influential 1758 publication *Systema Naturae*, this term was used to categorize dog-like carnivores, including the domestic dog, wolves, foxes, and jackals. Quite specifically, the domestic dog was originally classified as *Canis familiaris*, which translates to "family dog." Today, after several taxonomic revisions, the domestic dog is recognized as a subspecies of the wolf and is formally listed as *Canis lupus familiaris*.
context: In 1758, the taxonomist Linnaeus published in Systema Naturae a categorization of species which included the Canis species. Canis is a Latin word meaning dog, and the list included the dog-like carnivores: the domestic dog, wolves, foxes and jackals. The dog was classified as Canis familiaris, which means "Dog-family" or the family dog. On the next page he recorded the wolf as Canis lupus, which means "Dog-wolf". In 1978, a review aimed at reducing the number of recognized Canis species proposed that "Canis dingo is now generally regarded as a distinctive feral domestic dog. Canis familiaris is used for domestic dogs, although taxonomically it should probably be synonymous with Canis lupus." In 1982, the first edition of Mammal Species of the World listed Canis familiaris under Canis lupus with the comment: "Probably ancestor of and conspecific with the domestic dog, familiaris. Canis familiaris has page priority over Canis lupus, but both were published simultaneously in Linnaeus (1758), and Canis lupus has been universally used for this species", which avoided classifying the wolf as the family dog. The dog is now listed among the many other Latin-named subspecies of Canis lupus as Canis lupus familiaris.
question: What is the Latin word for dog?

encoded_text: Rather than viewing objects as spread across time, an endurantist holds that for an object to persist through time is for it to exist completely at different times. Under this view, each instance of existence can be regarded as somehow separate from previous and future instances, while still being numerically identical with them. Endurantism is considered the conventional view, flowing naturally from our everyday, pre-philosophical intuitions about interacting with objects as complete wholes.
context: The positions on the persistence of objects are somewhat similar. An endurantist holds that for an object to persist through time is for it to exist completely at different times (each instance of existence we can regard as somehow separate from previous and future instances, though still numerically identical with them). A perdurantist on the other hand holds that for a thing to exist through time is for it to exist as a continuous reality, and that when we consider the thing as a whole we must consider an aggregate of all its "temporal parts" or instances of existing. Endurantism is seen as the conventional view and flows out of our pre-philosophical ideas (when I talk to somebody I think I am talking to that person as a complete object, and not just a part of a cross-temporal being), but perdurantists have attacked this position. (An example of a perdurantist is David Lewis.) One argument perdurantists use to state the superiority of their view is that perdurantism is able to take account of change in objects.
question: Who holds  that for an object to persist through time is for it to exist completely at different times?

encoded_text: Deploying a reflector behind the active element of an antenna serves to increase the signal strength. A well-known example of this principle is the parabolic reflector antenna, which achieves an effective area far greater than what the active element could accomplish on its own. Notably, the reflector doesn't even need to be a solid surface—wire meshes or rows of passive elements work quite well, since gaps smaller than one-tenth of the wavelength have minimal impact on reflective performance. This also makes such reflectors lighter and less vulnerable to wind forces.
context: Reflection of the original signal also occurs when it hits an extended conductive surface, in a fashion similar to a mirror. This effect can also be used to increase signal through the use of a reflector, normally placed behind the active element and spaced so the reflected signal reaches the element in-phase. Generally the reflector will remain highly reflective even if it is not solid; gaps less than 1⁄10 generally have little effect on the outcome. For this reason, reflectors often take the form of wire meshes or rows of passive elements, which makes them lighter and less subject to wind. The parabolic reflector is perhaps the best known example of a reflector-based antenna, which has an effective area far greater than the active element alone.

encoded_text:
Within Whitehead's process philosophy, existence is fundamentally relational. He argues that any entity is essentially the sum of its relations to other entities — its synthesis of and reaction to everything around it. A real thing is precisely that which forces the rest of the universe to somehow conform to it or take account of it.

Following this logic, if something made strictly no difference to any other person, object, or entity whatsoever — meaning it held no relations to anything else in the universe — then it could not be said to truly exist. In Whitehead's framework, having zero effect on anything else is equivalent to non-existence. Relations are not merely secondary attributes of a thing; they constitute what the thing fundamentally *is*.

This perspective stands in sharp contrast to substance-based metaphysics, where a thing can be conceived as existing independently of its relations. For Whitehead, reality is deeply interconnected, and to be real means to make a difference somewhere in the web of relations that constitutes the universe.
context: In fact, Whitehead describes any entity as in some sense nothing more and nothing less than the sum of its relations to other entities – its synthesis of and reaction to the world around it. A real thing is just that which forces the rest of the universe to in some way conform to it; that is to say, if theoretically a thing made strictly no difference to any other entity (i.e. it was not related to any other entity), it could not be said to really exist. Relations are not secondary to what a thing is, they are what the thing is.

encoded_text: Heat can be fully converted into work in a reversible isothermal expansion of an ideal gas. During this type of process, the temperature remains constant throughout. No portion of the supplied energy gets stored within the gas itself. One should note, however, that this remarkable complete conversion applies specifically to this non-cyclic scenario. When dealing with cyclic processes, such as those found in practical heat engines, the second law of thermodynamics restricts how much thermal energy can become useful work. Every real engine must inevitably reject some energy as waste heat, limiting overall efficiency.
context: For "closed systems" with no external source or sink of energy, the first law of thermodynamics states that a system's energy is constant unless energy is transferred in or out by mechanical work or heat, and that no energy is lost in transfer. This means that it is impossible to create or destroy energy. While heat can always be fully converted into work in a reversible isothermal expansion of an ideal gas, for cyclic processes of practical interest in heat engines the second law of thermodynamics states that the system doing work always loses some energy as waste heat. This creates a limit to the amount of heat energy that can do work in a cyclic process, a limit called the available energy. Mechanical and other forms of energy can be transformed in the other direction into thermal energy without such limitations. The total energy of a system can be calculated by adding up all forms of energy in the system.
question: What can be fully converted into work in a reversible isothermal expansion of an ideal gas?

encoded_text: When successfully metabolized, dietary fiber can produce four kilocalories of energy per gram. context: Dietary fiber is a carbohydrate that is incompletely absorbed in humans and in some animals. Like all carbohydrates, when it is metabolized it can produce four Calories (kilocalories) of energy per gram. However, in most circumstances it accounts for less than that because of its limited absorption and digestibility. Dietary fiber consists mainly of cellulose, a large carbohydrate polymer which is indigestible as humans do not have the required enzymes to disassemble it. There are two subcategories: soluble and insoluble fiber. Whole grains, fruits (especially plums, prunes, and figs), and vegetables are good sources of dietary fiber. There are many health benefits of a high-fiber diet. Dietary fiber helps reduce the chance of gastrointestinal problems such as constipation and diarrhea by increasing the weight and size of stool and softening it. Insoluble fiber, found in whole wheat flour, nuts and vegetables, especially stimulates peristalsis – the rhythmic muscular contractions of the intestines, which move digesta along the digestive tract. Soluble fiber, found in oats, peas, beans, and many fruits, dissolves in water in the intestinal tract to produce a gel that slows the movement of food through the intestines. This may help lower blood glucose levels because it can slow the absorption of sugar. Additionally, fiber, perhaps especially that from whole grains, is thought to possibly help lessen insulin spikes, and therefore reduce the risk of type 2 diabetes. The link between increased fiber consumption and a decreased risk of colorectal cancer is still uncertain.
question: How many kilocalories of energy per gram is dietary fiber able to produce when successfully metabolized?

encoded_text: Fundamentally, aether was originally thought to be a rigid, indestructible material that seamlessly filled the heavens, leaving no empty space whatsoever. As understanding shifted, aether came to be regarded as an extremely rarefied form of air — indeed, the very name "aether" derives from a word associated with rarefied air. Later scientific thinking further adapted the concept, treating aether as a luminiferous medium through which light was believed to propagate across both terrestrial and celestial realms. Isaac Newton even relied on the concept to help explain phenomena such as refraction and radiant heat. By the 19th century, experiments were being conducted to try to detect this medium, though astronomer Henry Pickering noted in 1912 that the interstellar absorbing medium had characteristics of a gas with free gaseous molecules present.

Additionally, the concept informed Isaac Newton's explanations of both refraction and of radiant heat. 19th century experiments into this luminiferous aether attempted to detect a minute drag on the Earth's orbit. encoded_text: Chloroplasts originated through an ancient process called endosymbiosis, whereby early eukaryotic cells incorporated photosynthetic organisms into their own cellular machinery. Long before plants appeared, certain eukaryotic cells that had already acquired mitochondria through a prior endosymbiotic event engulfed cyanobacteria-like organisms. Eventually, rather than being digested, these captured cyanobacteria became permanent inhabitants of the host cell, gradually losing their independence and transforming into the organelles we now call chloroplasts. Algae were the first photosynthetic eukaryotes to benefit from this symbiotic partnership, and plants ultimately descended from lineages that inherited these vital organelles. Remarkably, the process didn't stop there — some algae later underwent additional rounds of endosymbiosis, engulfing other eukaryotic algae that already contained chloroplasts, producing what are called "second-generation" plastids through a mechanism known as secondary endosymbiosis.
context: The ancestors of modern bacteria were unicellular microorganisms that were the first forms of life to appear on Earth, about 4 billion years ago. For about 3 billion years, most organisms were microscopic, and bacteria and archaea were the dominant forms of life. In 2008, fossils of macroorganisms were discovered and named as the Francevillian biota. Although bacterial fossils exist, such as stromatolites, their lack of distinctive morphology prevents them from being used to examine the history of bacterial evolution, or to date the time of origin of a particular bacterial species. However, gene sequences can be used to reconstruct the bacterial phylogeny, and these studies indicate that bacteria diverged first from the archaeal/eukaryotic lineage. Bacteria were also involved in the second great evolutionary divergence, that of the archaea and eukaryotes. Here, eukaryotes resulted from the entering of ancient bacteria into endosymbiotic associations with the ancestors of eukaryotic cells, which were themselves possibly related to the Archaea. This involved the engulfment by proto-eukaryotic cells of alphaproteobacterial symbionts to form either mitochondria or hydrogenosomes, which are still found in all known Eukarya (sometimes in highly reduced form, e.g. in ancient "amitochondrial" protozoa). Later on, some eukaryotes that already contained mitochondria also engulfed cyanobacterial-like organisms. This led to the formation of chloroplasts in algae and plants. There are also some algae that originated from even later endosymbiotic events. Here, eukaryotes engulfed a eukaryotic algae that developed into a "second-generation" plastid. This is known as secondary endosymbiosis.

encoded_text: Yes, an unborn child can certainly face stress-related issues that may significantly affect their future cognitive abilities. Furthermore, studies reveal that offspring born to severely stressed parents tend to show heightened glucocorticoid responses when they themselves encounter stressful situations later in life, indicating a lasting biological vulnerability that persists well beyond birth. So even though the stress occurs before the child is born, the consequences carry forward, potentially making it harder for that individual to learn, memorize, and cope with stress throughout their lifetime. Both short-term and long-term maternal stress exposures are concerning, but prenatal stress is especially impactful because it shapes the brain during its most formative developmental window.

encoded_text: Largely, the term "Serbo-Croatian" is controversial today because of the prevailing belief that nation and language must correspond directly. In the aftermath of Yugoslavia's breakup, the newly independent states each sought to affirm distinct national languages — Croatian, Serbian, Bosnian, and Montenegrin — despite their high degree of mutual intelligibility. Nations that emerged from that era viewed a shared linguistic label as undermining their sovereignty and unique cultural identity. Even so, the term persists for practical reasons, as no succinct single alternative exists, though formulations like "Bosnian/Croatian/Serbian" (BCS) are increasingly favored in political and formal contexts such as the Hague War Crimes tribunal.
context: Throughout the history of the South Slavs, the vernacular, literary, and written languages (e.g. Chakavian, Kajkavian, Shtokavian) of the various regions and ethnicities developed and diverged independently. Prior to the 19th century, they were collectively called "Illyric", "Slavic", "Slavonian", "Bosnian", "Dalmatian", "Serbian" or "Croatian". As such, the term Serbo-Croatian was first used by Jacob Grimm in 1824, popularized by the Vienna philologist Jernej Kopitar in the following decades, and accepted by Croatian Zagreb grammarians in 1854 and 1859. At that time, Serb and Croat lands were still part of the Ottoman and Austrian Empires. Officially, the language was called variously Serbo-Croat, Croato-Serbian, Serbian and Croatian, Croatian and Serbian, Serbian or Croatian, Croatian or Serbian. Unofficially, Serbs and Croats typically called the language "Serbian" or "Croatian", respectively, without implying a distinction between the two, and again in independent Bosnia and Herzegovina, "Bosnian", "Croatian", and "Serbian" were considered to be three names of a single official language. Croatian linguist Dalibor Brozović advocated the term Serbo-Croatian as late as 1988, claiming that in an analogy with Indo-European, Serbo-Croatian does not only name the two components of the same language, but simply charts the limits of the region in which it is spoken and includes everything between the limits (‘Bosnian’ and ‘Montenegrin’). Today, use of the term "Serbo-Croatian" is controversial due to the prejudice that nation and language must match. It is still used for lack of a succinct alternative, though alternative names have been used, such as Bosnian/Croatian/Serbian (BCS), which is often seen in political contexts such as the Hague War Crimes tribunal.
question: For what reason is the term "Serbo-Croatian" controversial today?

encoded_text: The technique known as lossless audio compression produces a representation of digital data that decompresses to an exact digital duplicate of the original audio stream. The typical compression ratio achieved is around 50–60% of the original file size, as the complexity of audio waveforms limits further reduction.

encoded_text: When a memory is triggered by a time, it is known as **time-based prospective memory**. Given that prospective memory deals with remembering future intentions, time-based prospective memory specifically uses a time-cue to prompt a planned action. For example, if you need to remember to visit the doctor at 4pm, the scheduled time itself serves as the cue that triggers you to carry out the intended action, distinguishing it from event-based prospective memory, where an environmental stimulus like seeing a mailbox reminds you to post a letter.
context: Another major way to distinguish different memory functions is whether the content to be remembered is in the past, retrospective memory, or in the future, prospective memory. Thus, retrospective memory as a category includes semantic, episodic and autobiographical memory. In contrast, prospective memory is memory for future intentions, or remembering to remember (Winograd, 1988). Prospective memory can be further broken down into event- and time-based prospective remembering. Time-based prospective memories are triggered by a time-cue, such as going to the doctor (action) at 4pm (cue). Event-based prospective memories are intentions triggered by cues, such as remembering to post a letter (action) after seeing a mailbox (cue). Cues do not need to be related to the action (as the mailbox/letter example), and lists, sticky-notes, knotted handkerchiefs, or string around the finger all exemplify cues that people use as strategies to enhance prospective memory.
question: If a memory is triggered by a time, which kind of memory is this?

encoded_text: Homeostasis is defined as the ability of an animal to regulate the internal environment of its body, keeping major bodily parameters within a limited range of variation. The term itself derives from Greek, literally meaning "standing still." Pioneering physiologist Claude Bernard referred to this regulated internal environment as the *milieu intérieur*. The parameters maintained through homeostasis include temperature, water content, salt concentration in the bloodstream, blood glucose levels, and blood oxygen levels. The fundamental principle underlying homeostasis is negative feedback: whenever a parameter diverges from its set-point, sensors generate an error signal that evokes a corrective response, pushing the parameter back toward its optimum value. This principle is widely used in engineering as well, for example in thermostat-based temperature control.

encoded_text: A CCA protects private landowners by offering them regulatory certainty about future conservation obligations. encoded_text: Both the "antenna blind cone" and the "null" are names for the region along the axis of a dipole antenna's conductor where signals are very poorly radiated or received. Because a horizontally oriented dipole has a weakly directional radiation pattern, it handles signals reasonably well from most directions, yet along the physical length of the conductor itself, there exists a notable dead zone. In this area, the antenna's sensitivity drops dramatically, making it essentially unable to detect incoming signals or effectively transmit outward. Engineers and antenna designers must account for this blind cone when planning coverage, as it represents the fundamental geometric limitation inherent to dipole antenna designs.
context: One example of omnidirectional antennas is the very common vertical antenna or whip antenna consisting of a metal rod (often, but not always, a quarter of a wavelength long). A dipole antenna is similar but consists of two such conductors extending in opposite directions, with a total length that is often, but not always, a half of a wavelength long. Dipoles are typically oriented horizontally in which case they are weakly directional: signals are reasonably well radiated toward or received from all directions with the exception of the direction along the conductor itself; this region is called the antenna blind cone or null.

encoded_text: Using Planck constant values obtained through the Josephson effect and the quantum Hall effect to test the validity of those same underlying theories would lead to a circular argument. Because these measurement techniques rely on the assumed correctness of the Josephson effect and quantum Hall effect theories to produce their values, any Planck constant derived from them inherently presupposes the theories are accurate. You would essentially be using your conclusion as a premise — assuming the theories are valid to obtain a number, then citing that number as evidence the theories are valid. This kind of self-referential logic means such values can never serve as an independent verification of the quantum mechanical principles on which they depend. Other statistical approaches must instead be used to genuinely put these theories to the test, and so far those independent tests have not refuted them.
context: The theoretical difficulties arise from the fact that all of the methods except the X-ray crystal density method rely on the theoretical basis of the Josephson effect and the quantum Hall effect. If these theories are slightly inaccurate – though there is no evidence at present to suggest they are – the methods would not give accurate values for the Planck constant. More importantly, the values of the Planck constant obtained in this way cannot be used as tests of the theories without falling into a circular argument. Fortunately, there are other statistical ways of testing the theories, and the theories have yet to be refuted.
question: Using Planck constant values from these effects would lead to what logical issue?

encoded_text: The Estonian language derives its alphabet from the Latin script. Augmented with additional characters such as ä, ö, ü, and the distinctive letter õ, the alphabet was tailored to represent the unique sounds of Estonian. Letters like š and ž were also introduced specifically for loanwords and foreign names. Certain letters—including q, w, x, and y—are restricted to proper names of foreign origin, reflecting how Estonian selectively adapted the Latin writing system to suit its own phonological needs.
context: Like Finnish, Estonian employs the Latin script as the basis for its alphabet, which adds the letters ä, ö, ü, and õ, plus the later additions š and ž. The letters c, q, w, x and y are limited to proper names of foreign origin, and f, z, š, and ž appear in loanwords and foreign names only. Ö and ü are pronounced similarly to their equivalents in Swedish and German. Unlike in standard German but like Finnish and Swedish (when followed by 'r'), Ä is pronounced [æ], as in English mat. The vowels Ä, Ö and Ü are clearly separate phonemes and inherent in Estonian, although the letter shapes come from German. The letter õ denotes /ɤ/, unrounded /o/, or a close-mid back unrounded vowel. It is almost identical to the Bulgarian ъ /ɤ̞/ and the Vietnamese ơ, and is used to transcribe the Russian ы.
question: From what script does the Estonian language get its alphabet?

encoded_text: Horizontal gene transfer (HGT) is widely recognized as the primary explanation for striking resemblances between small portions of the genomes of otherwise very distantly related organisms. Through this mechanism, genetic material moves laterally between different species rather than being inherited vertically from parent to offspring. This phenomenon appears especially common among various microbes, where segments of DNA can be shared across remarkably divergent lineages. Furthermore, eukaryotic cells appear to have experienced a transfer of genetic material from their mitochondrial and chloroplast genomes into their nuclear chromosomes, providing vivid evidence of this process in complex life. Viewed broadly, HGT reveals that genetic similarity does not always indicate close evolutionary kinship, since even vastly unrelated organisms can share near-identical stretches of DNA acquired through lateral exchange.

encoded_text: Pāśupata Shaivism is the oldest of the major Shaiva schools. Lakulish systematized its philosophical framework in the 2nd century CE. Zealously independent in their theological outlook, Pashupatas rejected the Vaishnava doctrine of souls being permanently subservient to a Supreme Being, arguing that such dependence could never lead to the cessation of suffering. Whereas, Pati means the cause (or principium), the word designates the Lord, who is the cause of the universe, the pati, or the ruler. Pashupatas disapproved of Vaishnava theology, known for its doctrine servitude of souls to the Supreme Being, on the grounds that dependence upon anything could not be the means of cessation of pain and other desired ends. They recognised that those depending upon another and longing for independence will not be emancipated because they still depend upon something other than themselves. encoded_text: The temperature decreases as a result of rising from sea level into the upper regions of the atmosphere, a phenomenon explained by the adiabatic lapse rate. encoded_text: During the early 1690s, a significant literary and artistic quarrel erupted within the Académie française, pitting two intellectual camps against each other. Broadly, the Ancients argued that all worthy literary and artistic subjects should be constrained to those drawn from the works of classical Antiquity, viewing the Greek and Roman authors as unsurpassable models. Against this position, the Moderns championed the merits of contemporary authors from the century of Louis XIV, insisting that their own era had produced works of equal or greater value. The Moderns further pressed the argument—advanced notably by Fontenelle in his *Digression sur les anciens et les modernes* (1688)—that advances in modern scholarship enabled modern thinkers to surpass the ancients in knowledge. Essentially, the quarrel came down to whether literary excellence was forever fixed in the classical past or whether human progress made it possible for contemporary writers to rival and even exceed their predecessors.

encoded_text: The nucleoid is an irregularly shaped body located in the cytoplasm of bacterial cells. Rather than having a well-defined, consistent form, it occupies a region without a surrounding membrane. Its structure is quite different from the membrane-bound nucleus found in eukaryotic cells. Precisely because it lacks any enclosing membrane, the nucleoid has no fixed outline and can vary in appearance. Essentially, you can think of it as a concentrated but amorphous zone where the bacterial chromosome, along with associated proteins and RNA, clusters together. Some rare exceptions do exist — certain bacteria in the phylum Planctomycetes appear to have a double membrane around their nucleoids, giving those a more defined look.
context: Bacteria do not have a membrane-bound nucleus, and their genetic material is typically a single circular DNA chromosome located in the cytoplasm in an irregularly shaped body called the nucleoid. The nucleoid contains the chromosome with its associated proteins and RNA. The phylum Planctomycetes and candidate phylum Poribacteria may be exceptions to the general absence of internal membranes in bacteria, because they appear to have a double membrane around their nucleoids and contain other membrane-bound cellular structures. Like all living organisms, bacteria contain ribosomes, often grouped in chains called polyribosomes, for the production of proteins, but the structure of the bacterial ribosome is different from that of eukaryotes and Archaea. Bacterial ribosomes have a sedimentation rate of 70S (measured in Svedberg units): their subunits have rates of 30S and 50S. Some antibiotics bind specifically to 70S ribosomes and inhibit bacterial protein synthesis. Those antibiotics kill bacteria without affecting the larger 80S ribosomes of eukaryotic cells and without harming the host.
question: How does nucleoid look?

encoded_text: Lagrange's theorem is the foundational result that defines finite groups of order p, where p is a prime number, as necessarily cyclic (abelian) groups Zp. According to this theorem, the order of any subgroup must divide the order of the group. Because p is prime, its only positive divisors are 1 and p itself, which means there are no possible subgroup orders other than 1 and p. Consequently, every non-identity element must generate the entire group, making the group cyclic. Since the only group structure satisfying these constraints is Zp, any group of prime order is necessarily isomorphic to this unique cyclic group.
context: Mathematicians often strive for a complete classification (or list) of a mathematical notion. In the context of finite groups, this aim leads to difficult mathematics. According to Lagrange's theorem, finite groups of order p, a prime number, are necessarily cyclic (abelian) groups Zp. Groups of order p2 can also be shown to be abelian, a statement which does not generalize to order p3, as the non-abelian group D4 of order 8 = 23 above shows. Computer algebra systems can be used to list small groups, but there is no classification of all finite groups.q[›] An intermediate step is the classification of finite simple groups.r[›] A nontrivial group is called simple if its only normal subgroups are the trivial group and the group itself.s[›] The Jordan–Hölder theorem exhibits finite simple groups as the building blocks for all finite groups. Listing all finite simple groups was a major achievement in contemporary group theory. 1998 Fields Medal winner Richard Borcherds succeeded in proving the monstrous moonshine conjectures, a surprising and deep relation between the largest finite simple sporadic group—the "monster group"—and certain modular functions, a piece of classical complex analysis, and string theory, a theory supposed to unify the description of many physical phenomena.
question: What defines finite groups of order p, a prime number, as being necessarily cyclic (abelian) groups Zp?

encoded_text: The fundamental flaw in the light produced by an incandescent bulb is that it does not appear white. The spectrum emitted by a tungsten filament at typical operating temperatures is heavily skewed toward the infrared range, meaning the vast majority of the energy radiated is invisible to the human eye. For visible light to be produced most efficiently by a thermal radiator, temperatures of around 6,300 °C would be needed, but no known filament material can survive such extreme heat (considerably beyond even the sun's surface temperature). Because the filament operates well below this ideal temperature, the small fraction of energy that does fall within the visible spectrum is shifted toward the red and warm end, rather than matching the sensitivity profile of human vision. This mismatch between the emitted spectrum and the eye's peak sensitivity range results in very poor luminous efficacy — theoretically limited to about 52 lumens per watt even at tungsten's melting point, compared to the 95 lumens per watt an ideal radiator could achieve at the optimal temperature.
context: The spectrum emitted by a blackbody radiator at temperatures of incandescent bulbs does not match the sensitivity characteristics of the human eye; the light emitted does not appear white, and most is not in the range of wavelengths at which the eye is most sensitive. Tungsten filaments radiate mostly infrared radiation at temperatures where they remain solid – below 3,695 K (3,422 °C; 6,191 °F). Donald L. Klipstein explains it this way: "An ideal thermal radiator produces visible light most efficiently at temperatures around 6,300 °C (6,600 K; 11,400 °F). Even at this high temperature, a lot of the radiation is either infrared or ultraviolet, and the theoretical luminous efficacy (LER) is 95 lumens per watt." No known material can be used as a filament at this ideal temperature, which is hotter than the sun's surface. An upper limit for incandescent lamp luminous efficacy (LER) is around 52 lumens per watt, the theoretical value emitted by tungsten at its melting point.
question: What is the flaw in the color of light produced by an incandescent bulb?

encoded_text: Whitehead argued that it is neither philosophically nor ontologically sound to believe that a person remains exactly the same from one second to the next. He acknowledged that everyday language encourages this misconception, since giving each momentary state of a person a different name would be wildly impractical. However, he insisted that what we conveniently call a "person" or "material substance" is actually a generalized description of a continuum of particular, concrete processes. Just as no one disputes that a ten-year-old is quite different from who they become at thirty, Whitehead extended this reasoning to even the smallest intervals of time, arguing that true unchanging identity simply does not hold at any level.
context: Whitehead pointed to the limitations of language as one of the main culprits in maintaining a materialistic way of thinking, and acknowledged that it may be difficult to ever wholly move past such ideas in everyday speech. After all, each moment of each person's life can hardly be given a different proper name, and it is easy and convenient to think of people and objects as remaining fundamentally the same things, rather than constantly keeping in mind that each thing is a different thing from what it was a moment ago. Yet the limitations of everyday living and everyday speech should not prevent people from realizing that "material substances" or "essences" are a convenient generalized description of a continuum of particular, concrete processes. No one questions that a ten-year-old person is quite different by the time he or she turns thirty years old, and in many ways is not the same person at all; Whitehead points out that it is not philosophically or ontologically sound to think that a person is the same from one second to the next.
question: What did Whitehead state about the belief that a person is exactly the same from moment to moment?

encoded_text: Toyotomi Hideyoshi mobilized an army of 160,000 troops, consisting of both peasants and samurai, to send to Korea. Originally deployed in 1592 and then again in 1597, these massive forces were intended to carry out his ambitious plan of invading China through the Korean peninsula. These campaigns, despite initial Japanese successes on land due to arquebus expertise and battle-hardened warriors from the Sengoku period, ultimately failed owing to Korean naval superiority under Admiral Yi Sun-shin, Ming Chinese intervention, and Hideyoshi's own death in 1598.
context: In 1592, and again in 1597, Toyotomi Hideyoshi, aiming to invade China (唐入り) through Korea, mobilized an army of 160,000 peasants and samurai and deployed them to Korea. (See Hideyoshi's invasions of Korea, Chōsen-seibatsu (朝鮮征伐?). Taking advantage of arquebus mastery and extensive wartime experience from the Sengoku period, Japanese samurai armies made major gains in most of Korea. Kato Kiyomasa advanced to Orangkai territory (present-day Manchuria) bordering Korea to the northeast and crossed the border into Manchuria, but withdrew after retaliatory attacks from the Jurchens there, as it was clear he had outpaced the rest of the Japanese invasion force. A few of the more famous samurai generals of this war were Katō Kiyomasa, Konishi Yukinaga, and Shimazu Yoshihiro. Shimazu Yoshihiro led some 7,000 samurai and, despite being heavily outnumbered, defeated a host of allied Ming and Korean forces at the Battle of Sacheon in 1598, near the conclusion of the campaigns. Yoshihiro was feared as Oni-Shimazu ("Shimazu ogre") and his nickname spread across not only Korea but to Ming Dynasty China. In spite of the superiority of Japanese land forces, ultimately the two expeditions failed (though they did devastate the Korean landmass) from factors such as Korean naval superiority (which, led by Admiral Yi Sun-shin, harassed Japanese supply lines continuously throughout the wars, resulting in supply shortages on land), the commitment of sizeable Ming forces to Korea, Korean guerrilla actions, the underestimation of resistance by Japanese commanders (in the first campaign of 1592, Korean defenses on land were caught unprepared, under-trained, and under-armed; they were rapidly overrun, with only a limited number of successfully resistant engagements against the more-experienced and battle-hardened Japanese forces - in the second campaign of 1597, Korean and Ming forces proved to be a far more difficult challenge and, with the support of continued Korean naval superiority, limited Japanese gains to parts southeastern Korea), and wavering Japanese commitment to the campaigns as the wars dragged on. The final death blow to the Japanese campaigns in Korea came with Hideyoshi's death in late 1598 and the recall of all Japanese forces in Korea by the Council of Five Elders (established by Hideyoshi to oversee the transition from his regency to that of his son Hideyori).
question: How many troops did Toyotomi Hideyoshi send to Korea?

encoded_text: The Latin word for dog is **Canis**. This term was established by the taxonomist Linnaeus in his 1758 work *Systema Naturae*, where he used it quite broadly to categorize dog-like carnivores, including domestic dogs, wolves, foxes, and jackals. The domestic dog was originally classified as *Canis familiaris*, meaning "family dog." Over time, taxonomic revisions led to the domestic dog being reclassified as a subspecies of the wolf, and it is now formally recognized as *Canis lupus familiaris*.
context: In 1758, the taxonomist Linnaeus published in Systema Naturae a categorization of species which included the Canis species. Canis is a Latin word meaning dog, and the list included the dog-like carnivores: the domestic dog, wolves, foxes and jackals. The dog was classified as Canis familiaris, which means "Dog-family" or the family dog. On the next page he recorded the wolf as Canis lupus, which means "Dog-wolf". In 1978, a review aimed at reducing the number of recognized Canis species proposed that "Canis dingo is now generally regarded as a distinctive feral domestic dog. Canis familiaris is used for domestic dogs, although taxonomically it should probably be synonymous with Canis lupus." In 1982, the first edition of Mammal Species of the World listed Canis familiaris under Canis lupus with the comment: "Probably ancestor of and conspecific with the domestic dog, familiaris. Canis familiaris has page priority over Canis lupus, but both were published simultaneously in Linnaeus (1758), and Canis lupus has been universally used for this species", which avoided classifying the wolf as the family dog. The dog is now listed among the many other Latin-named subspecies of Canis lupus as Canis lupus familiaris.
question: What is the Latin word for dog?

encoded_text: An endurantist holds that for an object to persist through time, it must exist completely at different times. Recognizing each instance of existence as somehow separate from previous and future instances, yet still numerically identical with them, is central to this philosophical position on persistence.
context: The positions on the persistence of objects are somewhat similar. An endurantist holds that for an object to persist through time is for it to exist completely at different times (each instance of existence we can regard as somehow separate from previous and future instances, though still numerically identical with them). A perdurantist on the other hand holds that for a thing to exist through time is for it to exist as a continuous reality, and that when we consider the thing as a whole we must consider an aggregate of all its "temporal parts" or instances of existing. Endurantism is seen as the conventional view and flows out of our pre-philosophical ideas (when I talk to somebody I think I am talking to that person as a complete object, and not just a part of a cross-temporal being), but perdurantists have attacked this position. (An example of a perdurantist is David Lewis.) One argument perdurantists use to state the superiority of their view is that perdurantism is able to take account of change in objects.
question: Who holds  that for an object to persist through time is for it to exist completely at different times?

encoded_text: A reflector placed behind an active antenna element increases signal strength by bouncing the signal back toward the element. When the reflector is properly spaced so that the reflected signal reaches the active element in-phase, the signals combine constructively, resulting in a significantly stronger overall reception. Reflectors can take the form of wire meshes or rows of passive elements rather than solid surfaces, since gaps smaller than one-tenth of a wavelength have negligible impact on reflective performance.
context: Reflection of the original signal also occurs when it hits an extended conductive surface, in a fashion similar to a mirror. This effect can also be used to increase signal through the use of a reflector, normally placed behind the active element and spaced so the reflected signal reaches the element in-phase. Generally the reflector will remain highly reflective even if it is not solid; gaps less than 1⁄10 generally have little effect on the outcome. For this reason, reflectors often take the form of wire meshes or rows of passive elements, which makes them lighter and less subject to wind. The parabolic reflector is perhaps the best known example of a reflector-based antenna, which has an effective area far greater than the active element alone.

encoded_text: The first reference to the word "Christian" in the Bible is found in Acts 11:26 of the New Testament.
